title: Voter poll: What have US voters named the top issues at the midterms? - BBC

 Site search Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Documentaries Weather Newsletters Watch Live US voters name economy and state of democracy as top issues, poll says
 48 minutes ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Christine Jeavans Data Journalist BBC asks voters across US what brought them to the polls today The economy and the state of democracy have been named as the top issues for US voters, according to an election day poll.
 The survey - officially called the Voter Poll - asks tens of thousands of the American electorate their opinions and motivations, and providing a breakdown by age, gender, education and other demographics.
 Polling company SSRS collects data on behalf of a consortium of news companies, and the survey is a representative sample of American voters in the run up to the election, and includes exit polling of both early and on the day voters.
 Here are some of the breakdowns from the 2026 voter poll. Like all surveys they are estimates; the numbers are also likely to be updated as more data arrives.
 Economy ranked as top issue
 Reuters Some 39% of those asked in the poll of more than 79,000 people said the economy was the most important issue, while 33% put the state of democracy top.
 Following that, immigration was named most important by 14% of voters while healthcare, foreign policy and crime were ranked first by a lower share.
 Data suggests the majority of US voters have a negative view of the state of the national economy.
 Three-quarters of those asked said the economy was in a "not so good or poor" state with a quarter saying it was "excellent or good".
 Looking at their own family finances, 44% of people said they were in a worse situation than two years ago, 38% said about the same and 18% said better.
 Majority say Trump's policies 'worsened economy'
 Around two thirds (66%) of voters surveyed say US President Donald Trump's policies have worsened economic conditions in the country. 
 By contrast, 27% say Trump's policies have improved conditions and only 7% say the president has had no impact.
 People were also asked whether expressing support or opposition for Trump was one reason for their midterm vote.
 Some 44% said expressing opposition was a reason but 40% said he was not a factor. Only 16% of those asked said expressing support was a reason for their vote.
 Voters unhappy with state of the US
 Almost four in ten of those asked (39%) said they were angry at the way things are going in the US at the moment, with a further 37% saying they were dissatisfied.
 Only 18% said they were satisfied, and 7% of respondents felt enthusiastic.
 So taken together, there is a majority telling pollsters SSRS they are not happy about the current state of the country.
 Separately, a large majority, 90%, also said that government corruption was a crucial or major factor in their vote.
 Inflation has caused hardship for most Americans
 As well as broader issues, pollsters also asked about inflation and the impact of rising prices on people's lives.
 Almost eight in 10 voters (79%) said inflation had caused them and their family a severe or moderate hardship in the past year. A fifth (21%) of those answering said it had caused them no hardship at all.
 A majority of voters (59%) said they were "very concerned" about the cost of petrol and diesel and the same proportion gave this answer about the cost of food and groceries.
 More than six in 10 respondents (63%) said they thought that higher than usual prices were more because of Trump's policies.
 And 37% said it was more due to factors beyond his control.
 Majority say US 'made wrong decision on Iran'
 The voter poll also said that around six in 10 (63%) of those asked said the US made the wrong decision to take military action against Iran. Almost four in 10 (37%) said it was right.
 Separately, three-quarters of voters (74%) said the conflict was a crucial or major factor in their vote for Congress and a quarter (26%) said it was a minor factor or not a factor.
 Voting patterns differ by age and gender
 The voter poll gives an insight into how different groups of voters have cast their ballots. 
 Nationally, the data suggests women have backed Democratic candidates for the House by 59%, to 40% for Republicans. Men also voted for Democrats but by a smaller margin, 50% to 48%. 
 By age, around two-thirds of people aged under 45 said they voted Democrat. The middle-aged group, 45-64, backed the Democrats by 52% to 47% for Republicans.
 The over-65 age group was evenly split between candidates for the two parties. 
 White voters are evenly split between candidates for the two main parties, according to the poll. 
 All other groups have voted more for Democratic candidates, with Hispanic and Latino voters breaking for them by an estimated 64% compared to 34% for Republicans.
 Voters without a college education voted slightly more for Republicans in this election, by 50% to 48% Democrat, the survey suggested.
 People with a college degree have voted Democrat by an estimated 63% to 35% Republican. 
 All these numbers are for the national picture, voting patterns will vary state by state.
